In [[astrophysics]], the '''Bonnor–Ebert mass''' is the largest mass that an [[isothermal]] gas sphere embedded in a pressurized medium can have while still remaining in [[hydrostatic equilibrium]]. Clouds of gas with masses greater than the Bonnor–Ebert mass must inevitably undergo [[gravitational collapse]] to form much smaller and denser objects.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ebert |first=Rolf |title=Über die Verdichtung von H I-Gebieten |year=1955 |journal=Zeitschrift für Astrophysik |volume=37 |pages=217 |bibcode=1955ZA.....37..217E }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Bonnor |first=William Bowen |title=Boyle's Law and gravitational instability |year=1956 |journal=[[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]] |volume=116 |issue=3 |pages=351–359 |bibcode=1956MNRAS.116..351B | doi = 10.1093/mnras/116.3.351 |doi-access=free }}</ref> As the gravitational collapse of an interstellar gas cloud is the first stage in the formation of a [[protostar]], the Bonnor–Ebert mass is an important quantity in the study of [[star formation]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Carroll |first1=Bradley W. |last2=Ostlie |first2=Dale A. |title=An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics |publisher=[[Addison-Wesley]] |year=2007 |pages=413–414 }}</ref>

For a gas cloud embedded in a medium with a [[gas pressure]] <math>p_{0}</math>, the Bonnor–Ebert mass is given by<ref name=Draine>{{cite book |last= Draine |first=Bruce |date= 2011|title= Physics of the Interstellar and Intergalactic Medium|url= https://archive.org/details/physicsinterstel00bruc |url-access= limited |location=Oxfordshire United Kingdom |publisher=Princeton University Press |page=[https://archive.org/details/physicsinterstel00bruc/page/n483 457]|isbn=978-0-691-12214-4}}</ref>

<math>M_{BE} (p_0)={225\over {32 \sqrt{5 \pi}}}{c_s^4\over {(aG)}^{3 / 2}} {1\over \sqrt{p_0}} </math>

where G is the [[gravitational constant]] and <math>c_s \equiv \sqrt{kT/{\mu m_H}}</math> is the [[isothermal ]][[sound speed]] (<big><math>\gamma = 1</math></big>) with <math>\mu</math> as the molecular mass. <math>a</math> is a [[dimensionless quantity|dimensionless constant]] which varies based on the density distribution of the cloud. For a uniform mass density <math>a=1</math> and for a centrally peaked density <math>a\approx 1.67</math>.<ref name=Draine />
